National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) Islamabad, Pakistan moazam.fraz@seecs.edu.pk Abstract—Automated assessment is becoming more common in education because it helps ease teachers’ workload and makes evaluation more scalable. This doesn’t exactly show how students are thinking, or what kind of knowledge they are struggling with. To tackle this problem, we built an agentic system containing a two-step framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and improve question and answer pairs for vocational education. In the first step, we used the Llama-2-7b model to create an initial set of 2288 question and answer pairs. In the second step, we used the more powerful Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct model. We applied Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to a knowledge base of textbooks and online resources to refine and expand these questions, resulting in a final corpus of 4292 items. The prompt for this enhancement is based on Bloom’s taxonomy. It is used to map the difficulty levels of the question and answer pairs (easy: remember, understand; medium: apply, analyze; hard: evaluate, create). This enhanced Bloom’s taxon- omy framework also considers the type of knowledge involved: factual, conceptual, or procedural. Our results show that this framework not only scales up question generation but also makes the assessments more meaningful. It helps identify whether a student’s difficulties come from memory, comprehension or deeper reasoning, giving educators a clearer picture of learning challenges. Index Terms—Automated assessment, Bloom’s taxonomy, cog- nitive skills, educational technology, student evaluation. I. I NTRODUCTION Assessment plays an important role in education as it can be used to measure the achievement of students and provide feed- back for improved learning. It does not only determine whether learning outcomes have been met but also guides instructors in tailoring instruction to address the learners’ needs.

It does not only determine whether learning outcomes have been met but also guides instructors in tailoring instruction to address the learners’ needs. Before the automation of assessments, traditional manual grading was used which was not only time consuming and subjective but often inconsistent across evaluators. Recent advances in natural language processing and deep learning particularly with the rise of large language models, This work is funded by DAAD (German Academic Exchange Service) project titled ”Ba-Ikhtiyar Jawan: Upscaling & Digitisation of Vocational Education Curriculum in Pakistan” have enabled significant progress in the automated evaluation of objective, short answer and even essay type questions [1]. These systems promise efficiency and scalability, yet many existing approaches reduce assessment to a binary process in which answers are judged correct or incorrect [2]. For mean- ingful learning, it is critical to determine whether difficulties in learning arise from factual recall, conceptual understanding, procedural application or higher order reasoning. LLMs have the ability to process and analyze complex textual data, which they then use to offer a transformative opportunity to move beyond binary grading by providing context-aware feedback tailored to individual learner needs [3]. Bloom’s taxonomy provides a well established cognitive framework for classifying educational objectives into hier- archical levels of complexity [4]. This enhanced version of Bloom’s Taxonomy extends this framework by introducing two complementary dimensions which are Cognitive processes (remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create) and Knowledge types (factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive). This dual structure enables a better analysis of student performance as it moves beyond correctness to reveal both the depth of cognitive engagement and the type of knowledge being assessed.

This dual structure enables a better analysis of student performance as it moves beyond correctness to reveal both the depth of cognitive engagement and the type of knowledge being assessed. In the context of undergraduate education, the metacognitive dimension that involves reflection on one’s own thinking and the creation of new knowledge is often beyond the scope of the study. However, the remaining dimensions offer a stronger basis for structured assessment. By aligning of automated assessments with this framework, edu- cators’ can better diagnose learning gaps and design targeted interventions [5]. In this paper, we propose an automated assessment system that integrates enhanced Bloom’s taxonomy with LLM-based question generation and refinement. The system classifies assessment items not only by difficulty level but also by the type of knowledge they target. This allows instructors to identify specific weaknesses in students’ learning. Section IV presents re- sults and analysis of the system’s performance and diagnostic capabilities. Finally Section V concludes with key findings, limitations and directions for future research. II. R ELATED WORK This section reviews prior research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in education, focusing on their role in assessment, evaluation, and question generation. We organize the literature into five thematic strands: (1) LLMs for educational assessment, (2) LLMs as evaluators or “judges,” (3) question generation guided by Bloom’s taxonomy, (4) Bloom’s taxonomy as a pedagogical foundation, and (5) foun- dational advances in large-scale language models. A. LLMs for Educational Assessment The first line of research explores how LLMs can be applied directly to student assessment in formal learning contexts. Agostini et al. [6] conducted an evaluation in higher edu- cation where LLMs were asked to grade authentic student assignments. Instead of relying solely on surface level cor- rectness, these models were prompted using detailed rubrics and zero-shot instructions. These models then provide a score, an explanatory feedback and suggestions for improvement. The results demonstrated that LLMs can align with human raters. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 showed the strongest reliability. However, the consistency of grading varied depending on the complexity of the task, highlighting both the potential and the limitations of these approaches. This shows the practical utility of LLMs in reducing the workload of instructors while also providing immediate and formative feedback to learners. Beyond efficiency, the integration of pedagogical rubrics into LLM prompts reflects a shift toward using AI. It is not merely as a grading assistant but also a tool for fostering learning outcomes. B.

Beyond efficiency, the integration of pedagogical rubrics into LLM prompts reflects a shift toward using AI. It is not merely as a grading assistant but also a tool for fostering learning outcomes. B. LLMs as Evaluators (“LLM-as-a-Judge”) Zheng et al. [7] presented benchmarks like Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench. According to their results, GPT-4 attained 87–95% agreement with human evaluators which indicates that model can act as a substitute for knowledgeable judges in dialogue evaluation. Building on this, Chiang and Lee [8] investigated whether LLMs could serve as direct substitutes for human experts even in hostile environments. Their tests showed robustness across a range of inputs and confirmed a close alignment with human ratings. GPTScore being a probabilistic framework where LLMs act as judges across various tasks was introduced by Fu et al. [9]. GPTScore demonstrated the benefits of using semantic understanding instead of surface level overlaps by outperforming conven- tional automatic metrics like BLEU and ROUGE. ChatGPT was tested as a natural language generation evaluator by Wang et al. [10], who found strong correlations with human judg- ments in summarization and story generation. By using GPT- 4 in information retrieval, Thomas et al. [11] demonstrated that the model could forecast user preferences using chain- of-thought reasoning and structured prompting. EvalGen, a framework that methodically creates evaluators in line with human preferences for tasks like sentiment analysis and named entity recognition, was proposed by Shankar et al. [12]. The paradigm was expanded by Verga et al. [13] through the in- troduction of “jury-based” evaluation, in which several LLMs collaborate as judges to reduce individual biases and produce more trustworthy consensus. Beyond scholarly contributions, Samuylova offered a useful summary of LLM as a judge techniques such as pairwise comparison, reference free, refer- ence based scoring, and conversation level evaluation.

These techniques are summed up in a straightforward workflow in which an LLM grader processes student assignments to produce feedback (Figure 3). C. Question Generation and Bloom’s Taxonomy Parallel to evaluation research, another significant strand of work investigates LLMs for educational question generation, often guided by Bloom’s taxonomy. Duong-Trung et al. [14] introduced BloomLLM, a system that combines supervised fine-tuning with Bloom’s taxonomy to generate controlled questions across cognitive levels. Their results showed that ex- plicitly embedding taxonomy-based constraints improved both the relevance and pedagogical value of generated questions. Scaria et al. [15] evaluated the capability of modern LLMs to generate high-quality questions aligned with Bloom’s categories in the Indian high school curriculum. They found that while models could reliably generate factual and comprehension-level items, higher-order questions involving application, analysis, and evaluation remained challenging. In follow-up work, Scaria et al. [16] proposed automated strate- gies for question generation aligned with Bloom’s taxonomy, highlighting both opportunities and limitations in scaling these systems. Other researchers explored related approaches. Al Faraby and Romadhony [17] demonstrated that LLMs can adap- tively generate and classify questions across Bloom’s lev- els, underscoring their versatility in educational contexts. Li and Zhang [18] proposed a “planning-first, question-second” framework, where LLMs generate a structured outline before formulating questions, thereby improving coherence and align- ment with intended cognitive skills. Rao et al. [19] provided a comprehensive review of automatic Q&A generation methods, summarizing trends, datasets, and challenges. Mucciaccia et al. Bloom’s Taxonomy as a Pedagogical Foundation The foundation of this study lies mainly on Bloom’s tax- onomy and it’s later versions. Wilson [21] reviewed Anderson and Krathwohl’s revised taxonomy in which orignal Bloom’s hierarchy was updated by distinguishing between knowledge dimensions and cognitive processes. This enhanced framework provides a more sophisticated understanding that how learning outcomes can be structured and assessed. The taxonomy specifically focus on progressive levels of cognitive engage- ment that makes it suitable for guiding LLM-based question generation and assessment design. By incorporating these levels into model prompts it can be ensured that automated systems capture not only factual recall but also higher-order thinking skills. E. Foundational Advances in Large Language Models The advancements in large scale pre-trained modeks has increased the applications of LLMs in automated assessments and pedagogy. Brown et al. [22] demonstrated that GPT-3 can perform a wide range of tasks in a few-shot or zero-shot setting which revealed the emergent capabilities of scaling. Studies have validated that few-shot prompting with long- context models, can effectively resolve complex linguistic dependencies without the need for task-specific fine-tuning [23]. These findings catalyzed a wave of research into educa- tional applications, as researchers began to test that general- purpose models could be adapted for structured, pedagogically meaningful tasks. Further advancements in many models have improved rea- soning, factual accuracy and controllability which makes them more suitable for high stakes fields like education.

Further advancements in many models have improved rea- soning, factual accuracy and controllability which makes them more suitable for high stakes fields like education. In summary, prior research demonstrates that LLMs can act as evaluators of student tasks, chatbot outputs and information retrieval results, often achieving high alignment with human judges. In parallel, LLMs are increasingly applied to question generation tasks guided by Bloom’s taxonomy. Together, these two strands LLMs as evaluators and LLMs as pedagogical designers form the basis for our study, which leverages an enhanced Bloom’s taxonomy for automated educational as- sessment. III. P ROPOSED METHODOLOGY The proposed methodology builds on the use of a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that combines domain- specific data, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and the integration of Enhanced Bloom’s Taxonomy to generate high- quality assessment items. The overall goal of this approach is to automate the creation of structured questions and answers for the Auto-Electrician course, while also enabling diagnostic insights into students’ cognitive and knowledge-based abilities. A. Stage I: Data Collection and Preprocessing In the first stage, we collected a total of 656 YouTube video transcripts related to the Auto-Electrician course. This field was chosen carefully because it has strong balance between theoretical elements such as electrical principles, wiring diagrams, safety procedures and practical aspects such as diagnosing, testing and repairing automotive electrical com- ponents. YouTube videos in contrast to traditional textbooks offer vivid examples of practical applications, making them particularly suitable for vocational program such as auto- electrician training. From overall dataset, a subset of 262 transcripts was se- lected for initial processing. These transcripts were divided into smaller, semantically coherent chunks in order to be easily given to LLMs.

From overall dataset, a subset of 262 transcripts was se- lected for initial processing. These transcripts were divided into smaller, semantically coherent chunks in order to be easily given to LLMs. This preprocessing step was necessary because long transcripts often exceed the input length limitations of LLMs and unsegmented content may reduce the quality of generated outputs. The resulting dataset ensured that both theoretical explanations and practical demonstrations were captured in content. B. Stage II: Question Generation Using the Basic LLM The first stage of question generation employed the, meta- llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf model, which we designated as the baseline LLM in our pipeline. Following decoding settings were used while generation process: we used nucleus sampling with top p = 0.9 and 0.6 was the temperature. New tokens was set to 1024 and input transcripts were truncated at 4096 tokens This model was tasked with creating question–answer (QA) pairs directly from the preprocessed YouTube transcripts. The model generated questions across three levels of difficulty: easy, medium, and hard. This categorization helped in two ways. On one hand, it helps us to understand the learners level of understanding. For example, a student who struggles with easy questions is likely at the beginner stage and must strengthen foundational knowledge before advancing to more challenging tasks. On the other hand, it helps us to provide a tailored assessment pathway according to performance of student . In this first stage, the LLaMA-13B model generated 2288 QA pairs from the 262 transcripts. C. Stage III: Refinement with Enhanced LLM and RAG In the second stage, model filtered out low-quality questions and restructured them using Enhanced Bloom’s Taxonomy for pedagogical alignment.

C. Stage III: Refinement with Enhanced LLM and RAG In the second stage, model filtered out low-quality questions and restructured them using Enhanced Bloom’s Taxonomy for pedagogical alignment. For this purpose, we employed the meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct model, a more advanced LLM which was loaded using 4-bit quantization (load in 4bit = True) with a torch.bfloat16 data type to provide greater ca- pacity and reasoning ability. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework was included, which incorporated reliable domain specific resources to outputs. The RAG component included web-scraped technical blogs(e.g 2CarPros.com, HumbleMechanic.com), service man- uals, websites, and multiple textbooks on auto-electrician training. Stage IV: Integration of Enhanced Bloom’s Taxonomy The addition of Enhanced Bloom’s taxanomy is the key nov- elty of the the methodology. Cognitive depth and knowledge type were emphasized by this framework instead of relying on binary correctness as in traditional assessment methods. The enhancement introduces two dimensions: (1) cognitive processes which include levels of remembering, understand- ing, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating and (2) knowledge types which are factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive. Instructors can determine the type and degree of students’ knowledge more accurately along with the accuracy of their responses due to this combination of char- acteristics. This method supports more personalized feedback and instructional design which helps learners strengthen their cognitive skills and knowledge areas. We matched the difficulty levels produced in Stage II to certain cognitive categories in order to fully integrate this taxonomy within our system. Easy-level questions were in- cluded in category of remembering and understanding. They were restructured with verbs such as define, identify, describe, summarize, and interpret to represent the expected cogni- tive demand. As a result, instructors can diag- nose whether a student’s weakness lies in recalling factual knowledge, conceptual understanding or procedural applica- tion which is way better than simply marking correct or incorrect answers. The metacognitive dimension was excluded from this work. In a vocational program like auto-electrician training, it is neither feasible nor reliable to assess whether students can propose entirely new strategies or techniques and they are correct or not. The LLaMA-70B model expanded the initial 2,288 QA pairs into a more diverse and enhanced set of 4,292 questions. This significant increase reflects a broader coverage of the subject matter and demonstrates the value added by Bloom’s-aligned enhancements. E. Stage V: Diagnostic Insights and Limitations The proposed approach generates assessments along with diagnostic functions.

E. Stage V: Diagnostic Insights and Limitations The proposed approach generates assessments along with diagnostic functions. This method can provide detailed feed- back on students’ performance by mapping assessment ques- tions to both Bloom’s dimensions and difficulty levels. For example, a student may show strong factual knowledge but he can struggle with conceptual understanding. Alternatively, a learner may be successful in applying knowledge but fail when asked to evaluate or create. This diagnostic precision helps instructors to design more targeted treatments and enables learners to engage in regulated improvement. But this approach also has significant drawbacks as well. The most prominent is the removal of the metacognitive di- mension of Enhanced Bloom’s taxonomy. Although metacog- nition is a higher order of thinking that involves the creation of novel ideas. It is not feasible to assess these abilities automatically in the context of vocational training. More over, using YouTube transcripts as the primary data source although rich in practical content but it also creates potential inconsistencies in terminology and instructional depth. These limitations highlight possible opportunities for future work that include integration of expert-curated questions or developing mechanisms to evaluate metacognitive skills in applied con- texts. F . Workflow Overview The overall workflow of proposed system is displayed in Figure 3. Raw transcripts are processed by a base LLM to extract and generate base preliminary Q&A pairs in the first stage which serves as a foundation of assessment pipeline. The initial pairs are refined by an enhanced LLM which incor- porates retrieval-augmented generation (RAGs) to enrich the questions with external sources such as textbooks, blogs, and technical documents which improves the accuracy, reliability and domain coverage.

To guarantee pedagogical validity, the refinement process integrates Enhanced Bloom’s Taxonomy, which directs the restructuring of questions along cognitive processes and knowledge types. As a result, the pipeline allows for evaluations that are both scalable and diagnostically significant by classifying questions according to their level of difficulty as well as determining the cognitive and knowledge dimension they belong to. This ensures that the system can provide large scale evaluations that are both scalable and pedagogical aligned while still offering actionable feedback for learners and instructors. IV. R ESULTS To show the how well and effectively the proposed refine- ment pipeline works, we can make a comparison between initial Q&A pairs generated by the base LLM and their en- hanced counterparts generated after the integration of retrieval- augmented generation (RAGs) and Enhanced Bloom’s Taxon- omy. The following examples display how simple, raw and straightforward questions are systematically transformed into more comprehensive, pedagogically aligned pairs that not only increase clarity and depth but also incorporate difficulty levels and knowledge dimensions. The enhanced question answer pairs are rich in detail and they are more pedagogically structured and better suited for diagnostic as- sessment as compared to the simple Q&A pairs which makes them more valuable for educational contexts. V. C ONCLUSION This paper presents a novel and unique framework for aut- mated assessment where LLM integrates with RAGs using En- hanced Bloom’s Taxanomy. In contrast to traditional systems that mainly evaluate correctness, this pipeline generates struc- tured, pedagogically aligned question answers that distinguish between cognitive functions and knowledge dimensions. Find- ings of our method have shown that it produces scalable and diagnostically meaningful assessments. It provides practical information and insights of learners’ strengths and weaknesses. This framework has established a solid foundation for future work but reliance on YouTube transcripts and exclusion of the meta-cognitive dimension represents current limitations. Broader range of data sources, adaptive feedback mechanisms and large scale validation with student performance data to support pedagogical effectiveness of assessments can extend this scope. Overall, the study shows the potential of combining LLMs with well established educational theory to support both automated grading and deeper learning outcomes in a scalable manner. VI.
